Wyoming, North Dakota and West Virginia seem to always be in the 35-45% so most Americans there think that their Congress, president, and governor are not doing bad addressing global warming. I also notice that most states think that Congress should do more to address global warming.
What do you wonder?
I wonder why many Americans believe congress should do more rather than  presidents and governor. I also wonder why California is in the 55-70% most of the time. 
How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community because I can be affected by global warming because many people in my town live by water and sea levels could rise and destroy their houses.

This graph is showing us the percentage of americans who think their elected leaders should do more to address global warming in different states.

raw_comment: Looking at the data, I see that the majority of Americans believe that congress should do more in response to global warming. I wonder why the data turned out to be this way. At first, I wondered why people were not putting more responsibility on the President, the person who is supposed to have all the influence. Upon further consideration, putting the responsibility on congress does make sense, as they ultimately have the most power, and if united for a particular cause (global warming), then they could get the most done to address climate change. I notice that throughout all three of the visuals, North Dakota, West Virginia, and Wyoming appear blue, meaning that at most, only 40-45% of the state’s population felt that their elected leaders should do more to address global warming. I wonder why these three states appear to be outliers; what separates them from the other 47 states? I wonder if the people that responded to the survey and had their opinions recorded are a good reflection of the rest of their respective state’s population. I wonder this because of the mention that the most recent update to the maps was based on a survey of around 1,000 Americans worldwide. Did the survey encapsulate people of all social and economic backgrounds?

raw_comment: Having reviewed the visuals, I notice that Americans generally agree that Congress must put in more effort in addressing the issue of climate change, even in red states where this is typically of lesser concern. This intrigues me as I wonder where Americans stand in today's world on their trust in the government. raw_comment: When looking at the graph(s), I notice that an overwhelming high percentage of American people believe that congress should do more to address issues of global warming. ON the flip side of things, I observe that American's believe that the president should do the least, and thus be the least involved when it comes to issues regarding climate change. This was interesting, as I wonder why people shed the blame to congress at large rather than transitioning the blame to one singular individual. Human psychology suggests that when being hypercritical about generalized issues, people tend to shed the blame on one singular person representative of a larger social body. For instance, I am sure we have all heard "unemployment levels are high, it is person X's fault". Obviously said person is not sitting in their office, pressing buttons and making arrangements to increase the rate of unemployment, but serves a greater and more pertinent symbolic effect that America tends to elucidate. I am further curious to discover the reasons as to why so many American's feel like congress is at fault and should do more.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?

Most people from States in the Great Plains, don't hold the president responsible for issues with global warming. Most states agree that Congress and Governors should do more for their respective states about the issue.

What do you wonder?

I wonder why most people don't think the President should do more, the global warming issue isn't a State's, or country issue, it's a GLOBAL issue. Americans should want the President to do more because if we as a country start doing more it is more likely that other countries will follow suit.

How does this relate to you and your community?

New Jersey weather varies, and in recent years we have had very inconsistent weather to say the least. For example it has been raining for the last 6 or so days, the sky has looked dreary, as I look out the window the sun is out and it looks like a nice warm summer day.

What’s going on in this graph? Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.

"America! Do you hold YOUR elected officials responsible for the climate?"

I wonder what the requirements are to be considered responsible for addressing it, for example why aren't governors just as important as congress or the president. Why doesnt the middle see this more urgently. How many people did they survey.

Climate change is a GLOBAL issue and everyone's going to have to deal with the consequences of neglect and deciding not to pay urgent attention.

I saw that there were three states that weren't heavily biased in favor of any one side. Our nation believes that Congress is obligated to implement more constructive improvements.

4-Whose duty is it anyway? Who should be supporting climate initiatives?

What Do you Notice?

Looking at this graph, I can see that most states want the Congress to take action on climate change. According to the figure depicting public opinion on how much the Congress should do, 50% of residents in the majority of states want greater congressional action. Less states, nevertheless, favor placing the burden of accountability on the President. Less than 50% of the public wants the President to particularly do more about addressing climate change, as seen by the graph with more states being blue. And in the graph indicating whether the governor should take on more responsibilities, 505 people in most states agreed that he or she should.

What do you wonder? 

I'm curious whether there's a relationship between it and how people feel about the president. If you don't like the president right now, you might want him to do more, but if you do, you could think he's doing OK.

Relate? 

This concerns our community since we will be the ones dealing with the fallout if nothing is done.

raw_comment:
1. I notice that New York, Maryland, Florida, and California generally expect more from the government, whereas Wyoming, Montana, and West Virginia expect less. People are least satisfied with Congress overall, and don't expect as much from the president.

2. I wonder what the roles of Congress, the president, and governors have in the topic of global warming and which one has the most influence.

3. Global warming affects everyone by causing natural disasters and destroying ecosystems. This especially impacts the younger generations who will live to see those effects worsen.

4. "How Do Americans Think The Government Is Doing Against Climate Change?"

1. What do you notice? 
I notice that most of the country believes that congress or the governor of their state should do more than the president to address global warming. I also notice that California consistently has around 55-65% of people believing that Congress, the president, and their governor should be doing more while West Virginia consistently has a lower percentage of people wanting their elected leader to do more about climate change. 

2. What do you wonder?
I wonder how many people they actually collected data from and why is there such a difference between certain states consistently wanting their elected leaders to do more and other states that have a low percentage throughout each category. 

3. How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community because global warming is a global issue that needs to be taken seriously everywhere. it affects weather patterns, nature, our crops, humans, etc. It doesn't matter who takes action it just needs to happen before its too late. 

4. "Global Warming is Heating Things up but Who Will Make the change?"

raw_comment:
1) What do you notice?
The majority of Americans desire Congress to address global warming and believe its responsibility falls less on the president. In addition, three states consistently demonstrate no desire for such addressing no matter the elected leader.
2) What do you wonder?
What factors contribute to the selection of leaders? Why had those 3 states not approved of the given leaders to address global warming? Was it due to a lack of consideration for climate change, or because of the leaders? Why is it believed that Congress should address this matter, what assurance is given to have such trust in Congress? And how would they influence global warming? More so, what are any of the 3 leaders capable of doing to handle this matter?  
3) How does this relate to you and your community?
This graph shows a response to a global issue, an issue that will in time impact our community. 
4) What’s going on in this graph? Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
This graph demonstrates the varying opinions of each state in regards to who addresses global warming through a range of percentages. 
Headline: As climate change progresses, who will stand up?

raw_comment:
1. I notice three maps which address climate change communication; a nationally representative survey on global warming. This concept is modeled through modeled state-level results. We take note of the fact, that in most states many believe congress should do more to address global warming, as indicated by the abundance of orange in the first and third map. Within the second map, the nation seems almost split in a way when it comes to the idea that the president should do more (as we see both blue and orange). Also, we see a bar at the top which indicates the percentage of Americans who think their elected leaders should do more to address global warming. The more blue, the lower. The more orange the higher. Finally, under the bar there are numbers, but 65 is the only one with a % sign beside it.

2. I wonder why exactly most states believe congress should be responsible for doing more to address global warming. I also wonder what measures each one of these elected leaders (congress, the president, the governor of each state) have taken to address global warming. What factors contribute to the cases of global warming in each state?

3. Global warming should be a huge deal for all of us. I mean if we don't do anything to fix this issue, it poses as a life threatening situation. The chances of survival will start to slim in my community and just about anywhere around the globe.

4.  "Dear Elected Leaders, The Nation Is Calling Out to You!"

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I've noticed that more Americans believe that Congress and state governors should do more to fight global warming. In California and some northeastern states, 65% of Americans say that congress should be doing more. Less individuals, though, believe that the president need to take greater action to fight global warming. In the midwest and west, 40–50% of Americans think the president should take greater initiative.

What do you wonder?
Why do people not believe the president need to take more action? However, they believe that the governors and the congress should be taking the lead on this subject rather than the president.

How does this relate to you and your community?
This concerns me and my community since New Jersey thinks that both the president and Congress need to do more to combat global warming. However, ongoing awareness should be raised about this important subject so that even insignificant people like governors can draw greater attention.

What’s going on in this graph?
"President aside, Congress has taken control"

raw_comment:
1. I see that many Americans believe that legislature ought to work harder to address global warming. According to the graph, the key states where residents want Congress to take action on global warming are California, New York, and New Jersey. Wyoming, West Virginia, and North Dakota do not feel as strongly about the matter. The graph, which consists of three maps of the United States with the States shaded in different hues to represent percentages of people polled, can be used to assess whether or not congress, the president, or the governor should act more strongly. The percentages are between 40% and 65%; in addition, blue indicates the lower percentages and orange the higher percentages.
2. Why, in the opinion of their elected officials, do people not wish to make contributions locally as well? How can Congress help the global warming catastrophe, which has surpassed the impact of the president and governor?
3. The effect that this has on me and my community is that global warming is a matter that sometimes we are not aware of. For instance, the warming of the ocean is having an impact on aquatic life, such as coral reefs, which are crucial for supplying oxygen to aquatic and terrestrial life. New Jersey experiences inconsistent and changeable weather. It snowed on the first day of school while I was in elementary school, which is a rare and alarming occurrence.
4. “Which Politicians are Believed To Have The Greatest Influence With Global Warming Crisis?"

raw_comment:
1) What do you notice?

I noticed that the states that urge their elected leaders to address global warming are also the states that global warming is more prominent in. States like California, Florida, New Jersey ; etc all lie on coastal zones which can be affected by global warming. California and Texas go through excessive droughts and wildfires which can be caused by this as-well. I also noticed that more of the population in states think congress should do more instead of their own governor. Probably because they have more power.

2) What do you wonder?

I wonder as to why most people think Congress should be exerting the most effort to do more. Why do they have more faith in Congress than in the president or their local officials? I also wonder why there are only 3 states in blue on the congress map.

3) How does this relate to you and your community?

Due to the fact that global warming has become a problem that affects everyone, it affects my community. It's noteworthy to observe that the majority of respondents think Congress ought to take action on the matter more. We are all responsible for the condition of our planet in the long run.

4) What’s going on in this graph?
This graph is letting Americans know based off a survey taken about which parts of the population would like which part of our American government system to take control on addressing Global warming.

Global warming; Americas HEATED controversy

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
I notice that a lot of midwestern states believe that Congress should do more to address global warming. Additionally, it seems that a lot of northeastern states think the same. 

2.what you wonder?
I wonder what the states mean when it comes to "addressing" global warming. Do they want the leaders to make an effort to stop it? Or do they want the leaders to simply bring attention to the issue? 

3. This relates to me and my community because global warming is something that could have an effect on our futures. No matter what leader addresses the issue, progress needs to be made. 

4. This graph shows a map of the states and the percentage of each state thinking whether Congress, the President, or the governor should address global warming. A headline for this would be "Whose Problem Is It?"

I also notice that some states that lean strongly to the right did not vote strongly that any of the three government branches should do more for climate change. Strongly left-leaning states, like those in the northeast, did vote that more needs to be done for climate change. 
I am curious as to why the general population put climate change matters into Congress's hands and why they did not necessarily hold the president as accountable. I also wonder whether states that are more agriculture-oriented vote more strongly toward federal or state initiatives.
In regard to my community, I am curious why New Jersey did not vote strongly that its state government should do more for climate change, but they did vote more strongly that Congress should do more to resolve climate change issues. I am curious as to whether NJ already has strong climate change laws implemented and that is why it did not place as much responsibility on state governments. 
A catchy phrase for the title is: "We're All Responsible"

raw_comment:
Thanks to all students who responded.   Here are some of the catchy headlines that we received:  “Whose Job Is It To Handle Global Warming?” by EmilyAOSE of the Academy of Saint Elizabeth, “Who You Gonna Call? Who America Wants to Combat Global Warming” by Diego Lopez of Eaglecrest High School, "Heated Debate: Who Should Do More in Relation to Climate Change" by Giana in Ft. Lauderdale, FL, “Climate Change Action: A Major To-Do but for Who?” by May Wallace of Andover, MA, and"Global Warming Needs to be Addressed, But by Who?" by Jazarias of Perth Amboy High School, NJ
 
You can continue to post responses.  Please check back by Friday, Oct. 7 to see the Reveal with the free link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the maps and a few Stat Nuggets.

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).

graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

Signing off – Ben Kirk of Ithaca, New York, who thinks leaders at all levels of government should do more to address global warming and Greg Yarnall of Morristown, New Jersey who is happy it has finally stopped raining.

image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   - Three **choropleth maps** of the United States.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses **small multiples / faceting**: three side-by-side maps with the same geography and color scale.
   - No stacking.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| U.S. state | Categorical/nominal | Geographic region (state shapes/position on map) |
| Percentage of Americans who think elected leaders should do more to address global warming | Quantitative | Color/hue intensity on each state (shared choropleth scale) |
| Elected leader type / office | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into three panels: Congress, president, governor |

Additional visible text labels for the faceted variable:
- “Congress should do more”
- “The president should do more”
- “My governor should do more”
raw_comment:
States that are affected by global warming want more change. For example, California is always in the orange; 60-65% They want congress, the president, and the governor to do more to address global warming. Unlike in Wyoming and North Dakota where they are always blue in the 40% they don't think anyone should do more to address global warming, yet they still get affected by global warming. The choices are very different, more states want congress to do more, less states think the president should do more. The states on the outside of America are mostly in the 50-65% the states in the middle of America are mostly in the 40-50%
I wonder why the states decided who should do more to address global warming. What are the reasons behind what they picked? I wonder what the states want as a result? What more can congress do to address global warming? What is the reason the states don't think the president doesn't have to do more? What main difference can congress make that most states want it to do more to address global warming?
The data is asking how much global warming affects the community. It addresses the community so it is visible to see who is needed to create a positive change. Even if global warming affects all around the world, this data shows how different communities experience different things, and express who should be in charge/power to create this change.

raw_comment:
I immediately notice that more Americans believe that Congress should do more about global warming. More states in the northeast and west coast agree that Congress should help more with this issue, in comparison to the southern states. Some Americans do still believe that governors should do more, yet this percentage is nowhere near the amount of Americans who think that Congress should be the ones doing more. Very few Americans think that the president should do more to fight climate change. 

I notice that the percentages favoring more federal intervention aligned with the more democratic states, and the more republican states favor more efforts from the states to address global warming. Is there a connection between political parties and this data? I also wonder why states like North Dakota and Wyoming were outliers in the first map titled: Congress should do more. 

Especially in recent events, there has been more extreme weather, heat waves, rising sea levels, etc. We must be aware that climate change affects everyone. Our futures depend on what we do now to fight this climate crisis. 

Headline: Who Should Be The One Addressing Global Warming?

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that a larger percent of people expect more from congress than they do from the president or their governors. I also noticed that out of all three, the president is the one that people expect the least from, which is strange considering he’s the actual leader of the country. Although I presume that the reason Congress is depended upon the most is because they’re the only ones who can do things like make new laws to address global warming.
What do you wonder?
I wonder why people expect the least out of the president out of all three figures. I would at least expect people to want the President to address it more than a governor. raw_comment:
1.
People seem to think that Congress should be in charge of addressing climate change more. The number of people who believe the government should take more action to address the problem is significant, but it pales in comparison to what Congress could do. I also observe that a lot of individuals believe the president shouldn't take additional climate change action beyond what they have already taken. Additionally, it demonstrates that there are more states where less than 50% of residents think the president should take action to combat climate change. This may indicate that people don't anticipate the president to take action against global warming and don't think Congress or the executive branch should.

2. 
I wonder whether people's perception that Congress and the government should take more action to combat climate change than the president is because they think the latter is too busy "running the country" to be addressing things that people overlook ?


3.
This concerns me and my community because it's crucial to know who will be talking about significant problems like climate change, which has impacted our environment and planet, and if we don't take action, it will continue to have detrimental effects on it.

4. 
This graph displays the nations view on who needs to take additional action to tackle climate change.

Who should be our elected leader to manage the crucial climate change discussion?

I. What do you notice? 

People think congress needs to effect change more than the president. Maryland, New York, and California are the states that want the most change. West Virginia, Wyoming, and North
Dakota want the least amount of change.

II. What do you wonder? 

Why is the desire for change from the president so low? Why is the change from Congress so high? Why is New York so ready for change?

III. What impact does this have on you and your community? 

I live in MA, so it's interesting to see the views of people around me and people in other states.

IV. What's going on in this graph? & headline.

The graph shows the amount of people per state that want their leaders to do more about climate change. There are three different graphs, one for Congress, one for the President, and one for the Governor.

My catchy headline for this graph is:
"Is Global Warming A Hot Topic?; What Different States Think
About Climate Change."

1. What I notice about these maps is that it is mostly believed by the public that congress should be able to do more about climate change. I also notice that in light of the high percentile of agreement, many Americans are very split on the issue or tend to stay neutral, meaning that they agreed to disagree since the percentage was almost cut in half. Only a fraction of the states had an extreme agreement or a low percentage of agreement. 

2. I wonder why the percentage of people in the nation relies more on the governor doing something about climate change rather than the actual president? Also, why do people tend to vote for one extreme over another extreme, and not really focus on the person that can make the final decision, which is the president?

3. This can relate to the nation as a whole because climate change has changed the way we live our lives and the constant fear the people live in every day that a storm or the heat will destroy their town or state. It should be up to the people to decide what's best for the country because they live through it every day.

raw_comment:
1. I notice that the most commonly observed opinion in the graph is that congress should do more to address global warming. Slightly fewer people believe that their governor should do more, and way fewer believe that the president should do more. A few states in the north consistently show that they're not as worried about global warming compared to other states.

2. I wonder how region, political party, and the times over which these data were collected affected the data. Political ideologies vary by state and have changed over time. Additionally, climate change has been much more observable lately than in 2008. It's possible that if the data were separated into 4-year timelines adjacent to presidential terms rather than a collection over 13 years, the graphs could have a completely different meaning. Also, the data shows the overall opinion in each state, but what if the graph showed the data they collected in a way that would show the different regions where people had different opinions, rather than just state borders?

3. This relates to my community in many ways. One of them is my generation. The current generation mostly believes in the negative effects of global warming. Another way is the region/state in which I live, NJ. Most people in my immediate vicinity agree that Murphy does do a decent job concerning the environment, and doesn't completely ignore it like governors in other states.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I noticed that mostly all states, strongly believe that congress should do more to address global warming. A lot of states in the middle of the country believe that the president isn't the one who has to mainly address global warming. Also, the states that are on the coast, agree more than 50% that the congress, the president and the governors should do more.

What do you wonder?
I wonder why three of the states for all three charts did not change from blue to orange. Is it because the people in their state don't see global warming as a problem or is it because their states don't contribute to situations that worsen global warming. 

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community because in my state, the majority believe that the president and the congress should do more for global warming. In my opinion, I think our governor has been trying to cut down on actions that contribute to global warming but if higher powers were to enforce more action to address it, all the states would start to fix the issue. 

What's going on in this graph? Create a catchy headline.
In the graph, the percentages of which leaders should be addressing global warming in each state is depicted by color.

raw_comment:

It does make sense that people think (by about 60%-65% of the country's majority) that Congress should do much more to help climate change since Congress is supposed to be the voice of the people. This is similar when it comes to people's own state governments (with around 50%-60% of the country's majority agreeing), since they are more closely connected to them than the President.

raw_comment:
The darker the orange appears on the state, the more they believe that their elected leaders should do about climate change. The darker the blue the less they feel their elected leaders should do about climate change. The three different maps each represent their opinions on a different elected official, with the first representing congress, the second the president, and the third the governor. I noticed that the most people believed that congress should do more about global warming, and the least amount of people believed that the president should do more about global warming. 

I wonder why more people believed that congress should do more about climate change, instead of the president, since they are both at a national level.

I observed that there were three states which remained consistent throughout each of the different graphs. The first chart is the only one that has six states where 65% of the population believe Congress should address it. raw_comment:
What I notice:
The graphs drastically change colors through the three different groups of leaders. In the first graph, most of the population, almost all above 50%, think Congress should do more. Colorado, North Dakota, and West Virginia consistently do not think that the elected leaders should do more to address global warming. I also noticed that Most states don’t think the president should do more than Congress or their governor.
What I wonder:
Why do Americans think that the president doesn’t need to do as much more for global warming than Congress and the Governors? Do that states that had a lower percentage care less about government involvement, or do they think that the government is doing fine with global warming and climate change? Is this a general poll, or is this for a specific presidential administration? How does peoples’ political bias affect their answer? 
How this affects my community: 
My generation is entering the political scene and is taking on previous mishaps in the global warming crisis. My political leaders need to act to help save our planet from a global climate crisis. 
Headline: Leading the Climate Fight

raw_comment:
What do I notice?  
Between the three maps, I notice that the highest percentage of Americans want Congress to do more with respect to Global Warming. For example, in California, New York, New Jersey, Connecticut, and Maryland all have a percentage above 65%. 
What do I wonder? 
I wonder why people would not vote to have their president do more about Global Warming, as he would seemingly have more power than Congress. However, I believe they did this because of the legislative powers that Congress has. With Congress doing more about Global Warming, more can get done.  
What do I think is going on in this graph?  
How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community because the people that represent these percentages are citizens of the United States. All citizens of America are affected by Global Warming, therefore the way our government handles it is important to me and my community.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that most people across the US feel that Congress needs to do more about climate change. Others think that the president and the governor of their respective state should do more. States on the coast generally have more people that want the government across the board to do more about climate change. They are definitely seeing the effects of climate change through hurricanes, wildfires, and rising sea levels. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder if they think that the president is doing enough, or is it that Congress can make the actual laws and acts that will do something about climate change? (the president can pass the bills proposed, but Congress has to put together the bills and pass them.) 

How does this relate to you and your community?
Living in New Jersey, the coast is directly affected by climate change. During hurricane season, New Jersey often experiences flooding and a lot of rain. If nothing is done about the climate, parts of New Jersey will likely be underwater, as the sea levels are rising. 

What’s going on in this graph? Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
The Fate of the Climate is in Congress's Hands

raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's live moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s maps show how Americans feel about their elected officials – President, Congressional representatives, governors and local officials, with regard to addressing global warming.  

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?”, “What do you wonder?"  and “How will this affect you?”  Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in these “graphs.” We look forward to replying to your discoveries.

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the online article that included these maps.  

Note that you can get a link to your response (and replies made to it) to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

There will be no graph in the coming week.  The next “What’s Going On In This Graph?” will be released by Friday, Oct. 14 with moderation on Wednesday, Oct. 19.  The topic – immigration by country over time.  Keep noticing and wondering.

raw_comment:
I notice that more percentages of people think that congress should do more about global warming compared to the percentages of people that think the president or governor should do more.  I also noticed that based on the majority of the states, the least amount of Americans think that the president should do more about global warming. 
I wonder if these statistics have any effect on if leaders are changing the way they think about or act on global warming. I also wonder why more people think their governor should do more compared to the president. 
This graph relates to my community because of the effect that global warming has in my state. In my state, summers have become longer and hotter while falls and winter have become shorter and warmer. I would title this graph, "It's getting heated, who is helping?"

raw_comment:
What do I notice?
- Higher percentages of people overall think that Congress should be doing more to address global warming. 
- A majority of states close together in the middle have lower percentages of thinking the president should be doing more. 
- Hawaii and Alaska have lower percentages overall. 
What do I wonder?
- Do general politics affect a state's percentage on how global warming should be handled? 
- Does a state's climate affect whether or not the people want global warming to be addressed more? 
- What were these percentages like only thirty years ago? 
- What variables lead to seemingly random percentages in an area (Wyoming and North Dakota having lower percentages than other states near them thinking Congress should be doing more)? 
What do I think is going on in the graph? 
- I think that this graph is showing the percentages of different states' general populations' opinions on who should be addressing global warming more. The options are Congress, the president, and the governor. 
How does this relate to you and your community? 
- The state that I live in has generally low percentages except for thinking that Congress should be doing more. This relates to me and my community because global warming has had noticeable impacts on winters and fall in my state. 
Headline
- Who Each Area States Should Address Global Warming

raw_comment:
1. I observe that the citizens rely more on the elective leaders to start making a change rather than them starting to make a change. The citizens don't take the lead and become the leader in these types of circumstances, they will rather be the follower. 

2. Are the elective leaders really taking any actions when it comes to having global warming under control or are they letting us deal with the problem, however we can?

3.  This can be challenging to my community in many ways. Most of us rely on the fact that the president, congress, or even the governor will make a change to our real-life problems. They never seem to take action on the problem or when they do it might be too late. Just most of us are left hanging and have to take action of our own and start cooperating with the smallest things we can.

4. Why do people have so much hope in congress, do they really help us?

raw_comment:
1.) There is a heavy concentration between the densely populated states, (ex. California, New York, Texas, Florida) and their concern about global warming. I believe this is due to the major cities in the United States. I can also observe that there is a higher concern for global warming in the states along the coast whereas, the midwest states do not express as high concern.

2.) I am curious as to why the Midwest believes the president does not need to do more on global warming. This is surprising to me why the Midwest is not as concerned about global warming as it should be. In addition to that, it is concerning as to why the states that voted for Joe Biden believe he should be taking further action towards global warming whereas states that did not vote for Joe Biden do not think he could be doing more to act on global warming which is strange in my opinion.

3.) These graphs display how this is relevant to my community where in Massachusetts, a liberal state, we lean towards more environmental issues, such as climate change, and how we believe there needs to be more conversation and actions about these issues from our representatives (congress, president, and
governor).

4.) This graph is showing how not many states care that deeply about climate change and important environmental issues going on in the United States.

Coastal Climate CONCERNS, Central U.S. COMPLACENCIES

raw_comment:
1. I notice that most Americans believe Congress should do more to address global warming. I also see states like Wyoming, North Dakota, and West Virginia have a lower percentage of Americans who think any one of these organizations should be focusing on global warming. 

2. I wonder why the latter three states didn't seem to change much in the percentages of Americans who think their elected leaders should do more for Global Change.

3.  If you look closely you can see that in New Jersey there is a higher percentage of people who think Congress should do more compared to the governor needing to do more for addressing Global warming. It affects my community specifically because most of us are low-income families who will end up suffering the most if Global Warming continues to happen. 

4. "WHO SHOULD DO MORE? Americans decide."

raw_comment: As you can see on the graphs each one has a story to tell. This relates to and affects my community because it gives me an idea of where my state lies on the issue of global warming. This also affects my life because of the policy-making that could be about transportation. The reason why the colors are the way they are is because of the population of each state. The west coast and east coast states where most of the U.S population is are more towards warm colors. A majority of the U.S thinks that Congress and governors are doing a bad of addressing global warming. This is because Congress has a big part in the changing of law process which directly affects the global warming issue. This is similar to the effect of governors on a state scale they have some power to change the laws which is why most people believe that those too need to do more about the issue. A catchy headline that could be used is  "The world is heating and so are Americans' opinions about global warming."

raw_comment: According to the graph, many people think that congress should do more, their governor should do a bit less than congress, and that the president should do even less to address climate change. This is probably due to the president only being able to enforce laws, and the fact that congress can make climate policies to slow the effect of climate change. Local and state governors also have more power, as they can make laws more specific to how much pollution they are outputting. The graph does have a few inconsistencies, much like all data, like Wyoming, North Dakota, and West Virginia thinking that congress should do less, but this is probably due to their populations mostly being people who think that climate change isn't an issue, climate change not affecting them as much, or no one living there to interview in the first place. This will probably affect how policy makers choose how they vote and what laws they will try to pass, as higher percentage of people who think that something should be done will persuade them into making more decisions addressing climate change. These policies could make the climate more stable, and as such, will result in better temperatures for everywhere, and preservation of natural environments around the county. A good title for the graph could be "Something needs to be done: Who should be fixing climate change?"

raw_comment:
I notice that a majority of the country thinks congress should do more to address global warming. I also notice that a majority of the country thinks that their states governors should do more about global warming. Something else I noticed is that the middle of the country (Kansas, Missouri, Nebraska, Wyoming, South Dakota etc.) not as many people think the president should do more compared to congress or that states governor. One final thing I noticed is that in Wyoming and North Dakota not a lot of people think that anyone should do anything about climate change

I wonder why most of the middle of the country don't think the president should do more while thinking that congress and their governor should do more.

This relates to me and my community because the environment plays a major factor in Colorado's economy. Hunting and fishing alone bring in over 3.25 billion dollars and supports more than 25,000 full time jobs. If global warming effects the ecosystem of the Rocky Mountains it could be devastating to the Colorado Economy.

A title could be: "Pollution in Power, Who is to blame?"

raw_comment:
Based on the graph, it is evident that congress needs to do the most when addressing global warming. The graph suggest that a wide majority of the United States wants congress to do more on the oval warming issue. Citizens residing in California, New York, Connecticut, and New Jersey want Congress to do more to address global warming. However, North Dakota, Wyoming and West Virginia are less passionate about this issue. The midwestern states seemed to not feel as strongly to have the president do more about global warming. Once again, Wyoming, North Dakota, and West Virginia felt the most passionate that the president shouldn’t do as much for global warming. Based on the third graph, it is still a majority that the people of the U.S. want the governor to address global warming, with exception to North Dakota, Wyoming, West Virginia, Montana, and Alaska. One thing that I wonder is why Wyoming, North Dakota, and West Virginia are consistent in having less people vote that their elected leaders should do more about addressing global warming. Additionally I also wonder why the midwestern states feel less than the coastal states that the president should advocate global warming. This affects my community and I because it shows where our beliefs stand and how we would want our elected leaders to advocate for them. This graph displays the needs from each state and how Americans want their elected leaders to take action.

raw_comment: What I notice is this is political opinionated data. I notice how there are different colors to differentiate between those who want the President to do more, those that believe that their governor should do more and those that believe the congress should do more. It addresses global warming. It’s obvious people want to help climate change but don’t know where to begin with where or who. What I wonder about the data is how many people took the data. On what platform did the survey take place? How were the questions phrased to propose the matter? I do believe it relates to my community because we are very diverse and concerned for those who don't live with us. Not only the concerns, but the fact that weather is also changing around us. Most came to Vallejo for the gloomy bay area weather with nice sunny days, lately we’ve been going through heat waves and it's not fun. What is going on in the graph are people in America and their opinions on how to aid global warming. Some want the President to take action towards stopping climate change. Others want their state governors to address solutions. And the rest want congress to do something about climate change. To capture the main idea: Which branch is going to make the change?!

raw_comment:
1. Something I notice is that a high percentage of people believe that congress should do more for global warming. The percentage of people who believe that the governor should do more is more in the middle, the percentage is mostly between 50 to 55 percent. Something else I noticed was how Alaska changed, a majority believes that the congress should do more and for the president and governor the percentage of people that think they should do more goes down. 
2. I also wonder why more people don’t think the governor should do more since global warming can be a community/state issue? Florida has a big majority that believes the governor should do more. I'm wondering why there’s such a high percentage? 
3. This relates to me and my community because global warming can be a community issue. Each person in my community can do more to address global warming. However, I believe that the congress and the governor should do more to bring awareness or have a plan for each community, including mine. I feel like the president only has so much power and can do so much, it really relies on congress to do something.
4. The graph has a picture of the United States map and each of the three pictures falls under the category of the president, congress and governor should do more for global warming. Each state is color coded for the percentage of people who believe that the governor, president or congress should do more. 
Catchy Headline: Who Should be Doing More for Global Warming?

raw_comment:
1. Something I notice is that a high percentage of people believe that congress should do more for global warming. The percentage of people who believe that the governor should do more is more in the middle, the percentage is mostly between 50 to 55 percent. Something else I noticed was how Alaska changed, a majority believes that the congress should do more and for the president and governor the percentage of people that think they should do more goes down.
2. I also wonder why more people don’t think the governor should do more since global warming can be a community/state issue? Florida has a big majority that believes the governor should do more. I'm wondering why there’s such a high percentage? 
3. This relates to me and my community because global warming can be a community issue. Each person in my community can do more to address global warming. However, I believe that the congress and the governor should do more to bring awareness or have a plan for each community, including mine. I feel like the president only has so much power and can do so much, it really relies on congress to do something.
4. The graph has a picture of the United States map and each of the three pictures falls under the category of the president, congress and governor should do more for global warming. Each state is color coded for the percentage of people who believe that the governor, president or congress should do more.

Catchy Headline: Who Should be Doing More for Global Warming?

raw_comment:
1. Something I notice is that a high percentage of people believe that congress should do more for global warming. The percentage of people who believe that the governor should do more is more in the middle, the percentage is mostly between 50 to 55 percent. Something else I noticed was how Alaska changed, a majority believes that the congress should do more and for the president and governor the percentage of people that think they should do more goes down.
2. I also wonder why more people don’t think the governor should do more since global warming can be a community/state issue? Florida has a big majority that believes the governor should do more. I'm wondering why there’s such a high percentage? 
3. This relates to me and my community because global warming can be a community issue. Each person in my community can do more to address global warming. However, I believe that the congress and the governor should do more to bring awareness or have a plan for each community, including mine. I feel like the president only has so much power and can do so much, it really relies on congress to do something.
4. The graph has a picture of the United States map and each of the three pictures falls under the category of the president, congress and governor should do more for global warming. Each state is color coded for the percentage of people who believe that the governor, president or congress should do more.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
     From the graphs, I notice that a majority of the states want more of the officials to address global warming, with the exception of if the president should do more which the states are split on. Other things to note is that three states, North Dakota, Wyoming, and West Virginia, don’t think any officials should address global warming. Also the graphs also show that the states would prefer congress to do something over the president or their governors.

What do you wonder?
     From this graph, I wonder what makes the states say that they don’t want anyone to address global warming as it is a rising issue. With scientific proof that global warming will cause a huge issue down the road, it makes me think on why some states would be against people addressing this issue on getting it reduced or fixed.

How does this graph relate to you and your community?
     This graph relates to me and my community by showing what the people around me think of the problem at hand. Since the state I live in currently is California, it’s nice to see that a majority of people would like it if any of the officials would address global warming. 

What’s going on in this graph?
     Opinions On Global Warming? See what your state thinks!

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?

I notice that different states believe different leaders should be handling global warming better. Over half the respondents belonging to certain states like Wyoming, North Dakota, and West Virginia, don’t believe that any of their elected leaders need to do much at all to address global warming. While some states hold their governor more accountable than others, such as Florida. Though most states seem to agree that Congress, not the president, should be responsible for addressing global warming.

 2. What do you wonder? 

I wonder why these trends and exceptions exist in the way these states think of their leaders. I wonder if it’s due to cultural differences in the way different parts of the government are viewed, or possibly it’s because of the political situation of their state and how they relate to the currently elected leaders.

3. How does this relate to you and your community? 

This relates to me and my community because I live in an area that is adversely affected by climate change, and it makes me happy to see that most states agree that something must be done to address it.

4. What's going on in this graph? Create a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea.

“Congress caught lacking; not tough enough on climate change”

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?

I notice that different states believe different leaders should be handling global warming better. Over half the respondents belonging to certain states like Wyoming, North Dakota, and West Virginia, don’t believe that any of their elected leaders need to do much at all to address global warming. While some states hold their governor more accountable than others, such as Florida. Though most states seem to agree that Congress, not the president, should be responsible for addressing global warming.

 2. What do you wonder? 

I wonder why these trends and exceptions exist in the way these states think of their leaders. I wonder if it’s due to cultural differences in the way different parts of the government are viewed, or possibly it’s because of the political situation of their state and how they relate to the currently elected leaders.

3. How does this relate to you and your community? 

This relates to me and my community because I live in an area that is adversely affected by climate change, and it makes me happy to see that most states agree that something must be done to address it.

4. What's going on in this graph? Create a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea.

“Congress caught lacking; not tough enough on climate change”

1. **Chart type**  
   - Three **choropleth maps** of the United States.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses **small multiples / faceting**: three side-by-side maps with the same geography and color scale.
   - No stacking.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| U.S. state | Categorical/nominal | Geographic region (state shapes/position on map) |

| Elected leader type / office | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into three panels: Congress, president, governor |

Additional visible text labels for the faceted variable:
- “Congress should do more”
- “The president should do more”
- “My governor should do more”
raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?

I notice that different states believe different leaders should be handling global warming better. Over half the respondents belonging to certain states like Wyoming, North Dakota, and West Virginia, don’t believe that any of their elected leaders need to do much at all to address global warming. While some states hold their governor more accountable than others, such as Florida. Though most states seem to agree that Congress, not the president, should be responsible for addressing global warming.

 2. What do you wonder? 

I wonder why these trends and exceptions exist in the way these states think of their leaders. I wonder if it’s due to cultural differences in the way different parts of the government are viewed, or possibly it’s because of the political situation of their state and how they relate to the currently elected leaders.

3. How does this relate to you and your community? 

This relates to me and my community because I live in an area that is adversely affected by climate change, and it makes me happy to see that most states agree that something must be done to address it.

4. What's going on in this graph? Create a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea.

“Congress caught lacking; not tough enough on climate change”

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice? When studying the graphs I noticed that a majority of Americans don’t believe their president can do more to change global warming. 

2. What do you wonder? I wonder why both Florida and New York think their governor can do more when most other states are a much lighter shade of auburn. Also why does New Jersey have no data collected for whether their governor needs to be changed.

3. When you study the data we can see California is on average one if not the highest percentage of people who feel our government could do more. This is an obvious observation but I find it interesting that a state that loves their Governor so much thinks he could do anything wrong.

4. In this graph, Americans are displaying how they feel about their elected officials stances on climate change, whether they should do more. “How Does YOUR Community Feel About Your Elected Leaderships Stance on Climate Change?”

I wonder how the political parties of each state affect their views on who should do more.

If something is not done about Global Warming soon, my generation's grandchildren may not have a planet to live on and every child deserves a planet to play on. raw_comment:
(1) I noticed that several more Americans would want Congress to do more on addressing global warming while less would want the President to. 65% of California wants congress to do more, while around 55% want the president and governor to do something. I also notice that North Dakota and Wyoming remained around 40-50% for each categorical data. Another thing I noticed was the drastic changes in data collected for Congress compared to the President. 

(2) I wonder if this data will have any impact on our government due to the fact that they claim to fight for climate change, yet never proceed. Also, for states like North Dakota and Wyoming, I question if it were teens or young adults surveyed instead of adults, would the data look different? Personally, I believe there would be way more >50% with each state if teens and young adults in 2022 would answer. 


(3) As a person who advocates for climate change and insist for a greater awareness on this issue, this collection of data relates to my community and I because we are all being affected by it. We are noticing tides of our own waters getting higher and the drastic changes of temperature impacting everyday lives. Not only that, with the increasing amounts of hurricanes happening  around the world, all form of leadership positions should be forming a plan for the well-being of their people. 

(4) US States Answer: Climate Change NEEDS Attention!
